claims.claim: Bryce Lynch names a terse writing style as one of the things he looks for in an adventure module.
Bryce Lynch says in a comment on his own standards page that he loathes overly long backstory and fiction introductions in modules.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, comment of 19 April 2016 on 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: I LOATHE the overly long backstory

claims.claim: The tenfootpole reviewer who writes as 'The Pretty Girl' puts succinct-and-evocative at the top of her four-point Language scale for modules; the scale is hers, not Bryce Lynch's.
claims.source: 'The Pretty Girl', rating scale on 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.page: Review Standards, 'The Pretty Girl' section, Language scale

claims.claim: Justin Alexander defines boxed text in an RPG scenario as narration written in advance for the GM to read to the players.
claims.quote: a prewritten narration designed to be read to the players

claims.claim: Justin Alexander names the reaction point and says a description must not carry the world past it before the players may respond; he applies the test to a boxed passage he quotes from Journeys Through the Radiant Citadel.
claims.quote: the game world continue to move forward past the reaction point

claims.claim: A commenter on Alexander's post recalls a lost Wizards devblog article arguing GM-delivered descriptive text should stop at three sentences; the recollection is the commenter's, and the original article is not linked.
claims.source: commenter 'mellonbread', comment of 2 August 2022 on The Alexandrian
claims.quote: should never be longer than three sentences

claims.claim: David Noonan reports that from watching games at Gen Con 2005 he concluded a DM reading boxed text holds player attention for two sentences.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: If you’re the DM, you get two sentences. Period.

claims.claim: Noonan's stated mechanism for the attention loss is that read-aloud text converts the game's normal conversation into oration.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: Boxed text replaces that conversation with oration.

claims.claim: Noonan sets a three-sentence 2005 boxed text from Sons of Gruumsh beside a much longer one from 1999's Return to the Keep on the Borderlands to show that read-aloud text used to be far longer.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: Boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer

claims.claim: Noonan reports that players who heard boxed text still missed its factual content, naming room dimensions, exits and monster counts as what went past them.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: basic stuff, like room dimensions, how many doors exit the room

claims.claim: The Dungeon Master's Workshop close reading of King Bruenor's speech in Out of the Abyss objects that the passage is formatted like a novel, with a 'he says' attribution tag inside text meant to be spoken.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop, 'Dungeon Mastering 101: Mastering the Boxed Text'
claims.quote: structuring the narrative like it’s a book
claims.page: section on Out of the Abyss

claims.claim: The same close reading notes that Out of the Abyss's own instruction immediately after the Bruenor boxed text tells the DM to paraphrase it.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop, quoting Out of the Abyss
claims.page: section on Out of the Abyss

claims.claim: Dungeon Master's Workshop advises that a boxed text containing a paragraph break is usually already twice as long as it should be.
Dungeon Master's Workshop offers third-person objective and second-person subjective as two switchable registers for the same location description, illustrating each with a waterfall sentence.

Dungeon Master's Workshop reports that Waterdeep: Dragon Heist describes minor locations in mixed forms, a bookstore getting a short paraphrasable paragraph and a villa's great hall a set of bullet points.
claims.quote: A bookstore receives a short paragraph description

verdicts.trueWording: Bullet “Terse writing style” in Bryce Lynch’s list.
verdicts.note: Page header: “Review Standards / Bryce Lynch / What I’m looking for in an adventure module…”; the bullet list that follows contains the standalone line “Terse writing style” (with adjacent bullets “Evocative atmosphere” and “I don’t care about your epic backstory”). Raw HTML fetched from tenfootpole.org, HTTP 200.

verdicts.trueWording: “I LOATHE the overly long backstory and fiction intro’s”
verdicts.note: Comment on the same page: “Bryce Lynch says: April 19, 2016 at 8:36 am — I LOATHE the overly long backstory and fiction intro’s, but they are not on this list.” Author, date and wording all match; “in modules” is the page’s own subject matter (a review-standards page for adventure modules).

verdicts.trueWording: Language scale: “4 – Succinct and evocative”, top of four listed levels.
verdicts.note: In the section headed “The Pretty Girl”, written in her own first person (“When I built my rating scale…”, “My ratings system…”, “not the gourmand that Bryce is”), the Language scale reads 4 – Succinct and evocative / 2 – Conversational but clear / 1 – You should have hired an English Major to edit this / 0 – Very wordy/ incomprehensible. Four listed levels, top score 4, and the scale is explicitly hers and separate from Bryce Lynch’s bullet list above it.

verdicts.trueWording: “Boxed text … is a prewritten narration designed to be read to the players by the GM.”
verdicts.note: Opening sentence of the article, verbatim including the quoted fragment. Raw page fetched from thealexandrian.net, HTTP 200.

verdicts.trueWording: “what we’ve identified here is the reaction point”; avoid moving past it.
verdicts.note: Page: “What we’ve identified here is the reaction point” and “what you should avoid at all costs is having the game world continue to move forward past the reaction point without letting the players react.” The passage under discussion is the freeze-frame example labelled “(from Journeys Through the Radiant Citadel)”, quoted immediately above. All three limbs on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: “should never be longer than three sentences, because … players stop paying attention”
verdicts.note: Comment by mellonbread, timestamped “August 2nd, 2022 - 11:58 am”: “There was a lovely article in the old Wizards devblog … which was lost when they nuked their archives. The basic thesis was that boxed text (or any descriptive text delivered by the GM) should never be longer than three sentences…” No link is present in the comment, and it is explicitly the commenter’s recollection.

verdicts.trueWording: “If you’re the DM, you get two sentences. Period.”
verdicts.note: Live archive.wizards.com URL now redirects to the Wizards SPA shell, so the raw page was recovered via the Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20210713073031id_/http://archive.wizards.com/default.asp?x=dnd/dd/20050916a (HTTP 200, full article text). Byline “By Jesse Decker and David Noonan”; the first-person observer is identified as Dave (“because Dave spent a lot of time wandering around the convention hall at Gen Con”), the convention is named “Gen Con 2005”, and the quoted sentence appears verbatim under “Undercover Insight #1: Boxed Text = MEGO”.

verdicts.trueWording: “At its heart, a D&D game is a conversation … Boxed text replaces that conversation with oration.”
verdicts.note: Both sentences appear verbatim in Undercover Insight #1, and the article later calls it “the conversation vs. oration factor”, ranking it above two lesser factors — so it is indeed the stated mechanism.

verdicts.trueWording: “Boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer than it is today.”
verdicts.note: In the “Tangent Alert!” inside Undercover Insight #1. The Sons of Gruumsh sample quoted is exactly three sentences (oak doors / iron bands / All-Seeing Eye) and is contrasted with a much longer sample from “1999’s Return to the Keep on the Borderlands”. The page calls Sons of Gruumsh “a recent Forgotten Realms adventure” rather than printing the year; the article’s own dateline is 09/16/2005, which is what makes it the 2005 side of the contrast.

verdicts.trueWording: “missing the actual data … basic stuff, like room dimensions, how many doors exit the room, and number of monsters”
verdicts.note: Verbatim in Undercover Insight #1, immediately followed by the list of questions “from players who’d supposedly been paying attention” — supporting the limb that these were players who had heard the text.

verdicts.trueWording: “structuring the narrative like it’s a book … It doesn’t include things like ‘he says’”
verdicts.note: The Out of the Abyss boxed text is quoted in full on the page and opens “‘I’ve told the allies ye met tonight what ye told me,’ he says.” The critique names that tag directly and the article elsewhere says such text seems “as though it belonged in a novel”. Raw page fetched from dmsworkshop.com, HTTP 200.

verdicts.trueWording: “The first words after this boxed text read ‘Paraphrase Bruenor’s speech as needed…’”
verdicts.note: Full page sentence: “The first words after this boxed text read ‘Paraphrase Bruenor’s speech as needed to handle interjections by the characters’” — quotation verbatim and the “immediately after” limb is stated by the source itself.

verdicts.trueWording: “rare that a boxed text that includes a paragraph break isn’t already too long by half”
verdicts.note: The quotation is on the page, under the heading “Don’t Overdo It”, and the “usually” and “containing a paragraph break” limbs hold (“it’s rare that … isn’t”). But the page states an idiom, not a ratio: it never says such a boxed text is twice as long as it should be, and it also exempts introductory passages (“Aside from introductory passages”), a carve-out the claim drops. The advice is also addressed to people writing their own adventures.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the text is twice as long as it should be (the page says only “already too long by half”, and exempts introductory passages)

verdicts.trueWording: “shifting text from third-person objective (‘A 200-foot waterfall cascades down…’) to second-person subjective”
verdicts.note: Under the heading “Using Boxed Text Your Way”: “don’t shy away from shifting text from third-person objective (‘A 200-foot waterfall cascades down…’) to second-person subjective (‘You see a majestic waterfall hundreds of feet in height…’) if your players tend to lose focus”. Both registers are named and each is illustrated with a waterfall sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: “A bookstore receives a short paragraph description that is written to be more easily paraphrased”
verdicts.note: Full page sentence continues: “; a great hall in a noble villa has multiple bullet points describing the furnishings, the sounds, and the bodies on the floor”, prefaced by “While most important areas in the adventure are given the boxed text treatment, minor areas are often described differently” — every limb of the claim, including the mixed-forms framing, is on the page.
